topic: Auth: OAuth2, OIDC, JWT, RBAC, multi-tenant claims
why: The first two questions a customer's security team asks before a pilot may touch real data are 'how do our people log in with our IdP' and 'prove tenant A can never see tenant B', and the FDE is the person who answers both on the call and then makes them true in code that week. You do not get to choose the IdP (it will be Entra ID, Okta, Ping or a SAML-only ADFS), so you need a model of OAuth2 and OIDC precise enough to wire any of them in a day, explain PKCE and cookie attributes to a reviewer without hand-waving, and diagnose an `iss` mismatch from a token pasted into a ticket. Authorization bugs are the ones that end contracts: a cross-tenant read is a breach notification and a renewal conversation, not a bug ticket.
prerequisites: HTTP redirects, the `Authorization` header, cookies and TLS termination with `X-Forwarded-Proto`/`X-Forwarded-Host` from 'Networking' (topic 2): OIDC is a choreography of 302s, and the issuer URL changes the moment a proxy sits in front of the IdP.
FastAPI `Depends`, settings and lifespan from 'FastAPI in production' (topic 26): the verifier is a dependency and the JWKS client is lifespan state built exactly once.
Repository and domain layering from 'Production Python architecture' (topic 25): `tenant_id` becomes a mandatory argument on every repository method, sourced from the verified principal.
Docker Compose from 'Docker internals' (topic 5) to run Keycloak plus Postgres locally, and a working DefenderMate dashboard with at least one page and one API route to put behind login.

Cryptography at the level of 'private key signs, public key verifies', SHA-256, and base64url versus base64; you do not implement RSA here, you need to know why HS256 is wrong when the IdP is a third party.
Postgres transactions and `SET LOCAL` (row-level security is previewed here and deepened in 'PostgreSQL at depth', topic 29, and 'Data modelling for multi-tenant AI systems', topic 30).

subtopics.name: Authorization code grant, parameter by parameter
subtopics.learn: Trace the front channel and the back channel separately: the browser is sent to `GET {authorization_endpoint}?response_type=code&client_id=&redirect_uri=&scope=openid%20profile&state=&nonce=&code_challenge=&code_challenge_method=S256`, comes back to `redirect_uri?code=&state=`, and only then does your server (never the browser) `POST {token_endpoint}` with `grant_type=authorization_code&code=&redirect_uri=&code_verifier=` plus client authentication (`client_secret_basic` header or `private_key_jwt`). Know the invariants the AS enforces and you rely on: the code is single-use and short-lived (the spec recommends at most 10 minutes; Keycloak's client login timeout defaults to one minute), `redirect_uri` must exactly string-match a registered value, and `state` must round-trip unchanged or the callback is treated as a CSRF attempt. Be able to say what each of the four roles (resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server) maps to in DefenderMate: the analyst, the BFF, Keycloak, the API.

subtopics.name: PKCE: what it computes and which attacks it stops
subtopics.learn: Generate a `code_verifier` of 43-128 characters from the unreserved set `[A-Za-z0-9-._~]`, derive `code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier)))` with `code_challenge_method=S256` (never `plain`), send the challenge on the authorize request and the verifier on the token request; the AS stores the challenge with the code and refuses the exchange if the hash of the verifier does not match. Understand the two attacks it kills: authorization-code interception on public clients (a malicious mobile app registering the same custom URI scheme receives the code but not the verifier) and authorization-code injection on any client (attacker swaps their code into your session), which is why RFC 9700 and OAuth 2.1 require PKCE even for confidential clients that already hold a secret. Practise the 90-second version for a customer's security reviewer: 'we prove at exchange time that the same party that started the login is finishing it, using a one-time secret that never left our server'.

resource.label: RFC 7636 - Proof Key for Code Exchange

subtopics.name: The grant zoo and what OAuth 2.1 removed
subtopics.learn: Map every grant to a legitimate use and know which are dead: authorization code plus PKCE for anything with a human; `grant_type=client_credentials` for service-to-service with no user; device authorization (RFC 8628: `device_code`, `user_code`, poll with `grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code`) for CLIs and kiosks; `grant_type=refresh_token` to extend sessions. Explain why implicit (`response_type=token`, token in the URL fragment, no client authentication, leaks through history and Referer) and resource-owner password (`grant_type=password`, teaches users to type IdP passwords into apps, breaks MFA and federation) were removed from OAuth 2.1, and that Keycloak's 'Direct access grants' checkbox is the password grant and must stay off on production clients. Be ready to push back when a customer's legacy integration insists on the password grant: offer client credentials or device flow instead.

subtopics.name: OIDC on top of OAuth: ID token, nonce, discovery, sub
subtopics.learn: Adding `scope=openid` turns an OAuth delegation into an authentication event: the token response gains an `id_token` (a JWT whose `aud` is your client_id, asserting who authenticated and when via `auth_time`, `acr`, `amr`) while the `access_token` remains the credential for the API and may be opaque. Fetch `{issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration` and read `authorization_endpoint`, `token_endpoint`, `jwks_uri`, `end_session_endpoint`, `userinfo_endpoint`, `code_challenge_methods_supported` and `id_token_signing_alg_values_supported`; for Keycloak the issuer is `https://<host>/realms/<realm>` and `iss` must match byte-for-byte, including scheme and no trailing slash. Generate a `nonce` per login, store it in the pre-login session, and reject an ID token whose `nonce` claim differs (replay defence). Key the local user row on (`iss`, `sub`) because `sub` is the only claim guaranteed stable and unique per issuer; `email` can change, be unverified (`email_verified=false`) or be reassigned, and `preferred_username` is display text.

subtopics.name: JWT structure and the non-negotiable validation checklist
subtopics.learn: Read a JWS compact token as `BASE64URL(header).BASE64URL(payload).BASE64URL(signature)`; the header carries `alg`, `typ`, `kid`; the payload carries the registered claims `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `exp`, `nbf`, `iat`, `jti`. Implement validation in this order and be able to justify each step: pin the allowed algorithms server-side (`algorithms=['RS256']` or ES256; never let the token's `alg` decide, which kills `alg=none` and the RS256-to-HS256 key-confusion attack where the public key is used as an HMAC secret), resolve the key by `kid` from a trusted JWKS (ignore `jku`, `x5u` and embedded `jwk` headers), verify the signature, then `iss` exact, `aud` contains your API's identifier, `exp` and `nbf` with a leeway of at most 30-60 seconds, and require `sub`, `exp`, `iat` to be present. Know that JWS is signed-not-encrypted (anyone can read the payload, so no secrets in claims), JWE is encrypted and rare for access tokens, and that base64url differs from base64 (`-_` not `+/`, no padding), which is why a naive `base64 -d` fails on tokens.

resource.label: RFC 8725 - JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

subtopics.name: JWKS fetching, kid-based caching and key rotation
subtopics.learn: The IdP publishes public keys at `jwks_uri` as `{"keys":[{"kty":"RSA","kid":"...","use":"sig","alg":"RS256","n":"...","e":"AQAB"}]}` (Keycloak: `/realms/<realm>/protocol/openid-connect/certs`); your verifier must cache keys by `kid`, refetch once on an unknown `kid` (rate-limited, no more than about once a minute) so scheduled rotation causes zero 401s, and keep serving cached keys if the IdP is unreachable rather than failing the read path closed. Use `jwt.PyJWKClient(jwks_uri, cache_keys=True, lifespan=300)` with `get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)` in Python, or `createRemoteJWKSet(new URL(jwks_uri), {cooldownDuration, cacheMaxAge})` with `jwtVerify` from `jose` in Node; construct the client once at startup (FastAPI lifespan, topic 26), never per request. Rehearse a rotation in Keycloak: Realm settings -> Keys -> add a new `rsa-generated` provider with a higher priority, watch the JWKS document list both keys, confirm new tokens carry the new `kid`, then remove the old provider only after the longest token lifetime has elapsed.

resource.label: PyJWT usage docs - retrieving signing keys from a JWKS endpoint

subtopics.name: Token lifetimes, refresh rotation, revocation and introspection
subtopics.learn: Set the access-token lifetime to 5-15 minutes and accept that a stateless JWT cannot be recalled before `exp`; everything longer-lived is a refresh token that is exchanged with `grant_type=refresh_token` and rotated on every use (Keycloak: Realm settings -> Tokens -> 'Revoke Refresh Token' ON with 'Refresh Token Max Reuse' 0), so a replayed refresh token is detected and the whole token family is revoked. Use RFC 7009 `POST {revocation_endpoint}` with `token` and `token_type_hint=refresh_token` on logout, and RFC 7662 `POST {introspection_endpoint}` (authenticated as the resource server) to get `{"active":true,"scope":...,"exp":...}` for the few operations where 'revoked 30 seconds ago' must be honoured (tenant deletion, API-key rotation) instead of stretching every token to a day. Know that `offline_access` produces offline tokens in Keycloak for background jobs with their own idle rules, and that SSO Session Idle/Max and Client Session Idle/Max cap what any refresh can extend.

subtopics.name: Browser clients: the BFF pattern, cookie attributes and CSRF
subtopics.learn: Decide where tokens live before writing a line of frontend: a SPA holding tokens in `localStorage` hands them to any XSS payload, holding them in memory still exposes them to same-origin script, so the browser-based-apps BCP recommends the backend-for-frontend pattern: the server does the code exchange, stores access and refresh tokens server-side (Redis, topic 31) keyed by an opaque session id, and the browser holds only `Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=<random>; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/`. Know exactly what each attribute does: `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from `document.cookie`, `Secure` restricts it to TLS, the `__Host-` prefix forbids `Domain=` and forces `Path=/`, and `SameSite=Lax` blocks cross-site POST cookies but still sends on top-level GET navigations, so state-changing routes must also check `Origin` or `Sec-Fetch-Site`, or use a double-submit token. Remember the 4096-byte cookie cap: never put a Keycloak access token carrying roles and group paths into a cookie; store the token server-side and give the browser only the session id.

resource.label: IETF draft - OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications

subtopics.name: Standing up Keycloak: realm, clients, scopes, roles, export and import
subtopics.learn: Run `docker run -p 8080:8080 -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=... quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.x start-dev`, create realm `defendermate`, a confidential OIDC client `defendermate-bff` (Client authentication ON, Standard flow ON, Direct access grants OFF, exact Valid redirect URIs, Web origins set, PKCE method S256 under Advanced) and a second client `defendermate-api` that exists so it can appear in `aud`. Distinguish realm roles from client roles (`realm_access.roles` vs `resource_access.<client>.roles` in the token), composite roles, groups with role mappings, and client scopes (default vs optional: `roles`, `profile`, `email`, `offline_access`). Make it reproducible: `kc.sh export --dir /opt/keycloak/data/export --realm defendermate --users realm_file`, commit the JSON, and start with `--import-realm` reading `/opt/keycloak/data/import/` in Compose so a fresh checkout logs in with no clicking. For production run `start` not `start-dev`: `KC_DB=postgres`, `KC_DB_URL`, `KC_HOSTNAME`, `KC_PROXY_HEADERS=xforwarded`, and `KC_HTTP_ENABLED=true` only behind a TLS-terminating proxy.

subtopics.name: Putting tenant and audience claims into the token
subtopics.learn: By default a Keycloak access token's `aud` is `account`, not your API, so add an 'Audience' protocol mapper (Included Client Audience = `defendermate-api`, Add to access token ON) or your `aud` check fails the day you enable it. Model the tenant one of four ways and be able to argue the trade-off: a `tenant_id` user attribute surfaced by a 'User Attribute' mapper (simplest; one tenant per user), groups as tenants via a 'Group Membership' mapper (`/tenants/acme`, full path ON), Keycloak Organizations (26+) exposing an `organization` claim through the `organization` client scope for many-to-many membership, or one realm per tenant (hardest isolation, N discovery URLs, N admin surfaces). For users in several tenants prefer a token bound to one tenant at a time (a tenant picker that re-authorizes) over a `tenants: [...]` array plus an `X-Tenant-Id` header; if you must use the header, the API intersects it with the claim and never trusts it alone. Keep tokens small: turn 'Full scope allowed' OFF on the client, map only the roles the API needs, and never map every group path, or a 50-group admin gets a 6 KB token.

resource.label: Keycloak Server Administration Guide (protocol mappers, roles, groups, organizations)

subtopics.name: Bearer token usage and the JWT access-token profile
subtopics.learn: Accept tokens only in `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (RFC 6750); never from a query string (leaks into access logs, Referer and browser history) and never from a cookie on a pure API. Return `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="defendermate", error="invalid_token", error_description="..."` for missing, malformed, expired or badly-signed tokens, and `403` with `error="insufficient_scope", scope="alerts:write"` when the token is valid but lacks scope; the distinction matters because well-behaved clients refresh and retry on 401 and must not retry on 403. Read RFC 9068 so you recognise a well-formed JWT access token: header `typ: at+jwt`, required `iss`, `exp`, `aud`, `sub`, `client_id`, `iat`, `jti`; checking `typ` is a cheap way to refuse an ID token presented to the API, the single most common frontend mistake.

subtopics.name: The FastAPI verifier dependency and the Principal object
subtopics.learn: Build one dependency and put nothing auth-related anywhere else: `HTTPBearer(auto_error=False)` extracts the header, `jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token)` resolves the key, `jwt.decode(token, key.key, algorithms=['RS256'], audience='defendermate-api', issuer=settings.issuer, leeway=30, options={'require': ['exp', 'iat', 'sub']})` validates, and the claims are mapped into a frozen `Principal(sub, tenant_id, roles, scopes, sid)` dataclass. Catch `jwt.ExpiredSignatureError`, `jwt.InvalidAudienceError`, `jwt.InvalidIssuerError` and `jwt.PyJWKClientError` separately and turn each into a 401 with the matching `error_description`, so field debugging is one log line rather than a stack trace. Layer authorization as further dependencies (`require_role('tenant_admin')`, `require_scope('alerts:write')`) that take `Principal` via `Depends` and raise 403; pass `Principal` to handlers and repositories as a parameter, never through a global or a thread-local. Same shape in Node for the DefenderMate API: `jose.jwtVerify(token, remoteJwks, {issuer, audience, algorithms: ['RS256']})` in a middleware that attaches `req.principal`.

subtopics.name: RBAC design: roles in the token, permissions in the API
subtopics.learn: Keep the IdP's vocabulary coarse (`tenant_admin`, `analyst`, `viewer`, `integration`) and map roles to fine permissions (`alerts:read`, `alerts:reclassify`, `hubspot:write`, `tenant:manage`) inside the API in one table or module, so adding a permission is a deploy, not an IdP change plus a token reissue. Separate the three questions a request must answer: authentication (who: `sub`), delegation (what the client was allowed to ask for: `scope`) and authorization (what this user may do here: roles -> permissions), and check scope and permission both when the caller is a third-party client. Make every role tenant-relative: `tenant_admin` means admin of the tenant in the token, never of all tenants; a platform-operator role for your own staff must be a distinct realm role the API handles explicitly and audits loudly. Deny by default, centralise decisions in `require(perm)` so there is no `if 'admin' in roles` scattered through handlers, and know where RBAC stops working: per-object sharing and delegation ('let this contractor see only alerts from source X'), which is ABAC or relationship-based (Zanzibar-style OpenFGA/SpiceDB) territory.

subtopics.name: Tenant enforcement in the API and the data layer (BOLA)
subtopics.learn: Broken object-level authorization is the number one API risk because it is the default outcome of writing `SELECT * FROM alerts WHERE id = :id`: every repository method takes `tenant_id` as a mandatory first argument sourced from `Principal`, every query carries `AND tenant_id = :tenant_id`, and any tenant identifier in the URL or body is compared against the token and rejected on mismatch. Decide and document 404 vs 403 on mismatch: 404 hides existence and defeats ID enumeration, 403 is more debuggable; pick one per API and test it. Add Postgres row-level security as the second lock: `ALTER TABLE alerts ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; ALTER TABLE alerts FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON alerts USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)::uuid);` with the API running `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = :tenant_id` inside each transaction as a database role that is not the table owner (owners bypass RLS unless FORCE is set; superusers and `BYPASSRLS` roles always bypass). Carry `tenant_id` explicitly into background work (Temporal activity inputs, Kafka message keys) because there is no request principal there. Write the authorization-matrix test first: two tenants x every role x every route asserting the exact status code, plus URL-swap and header-spoof cases.

resource.label: OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 - API1 Broken Object Level Authorization

subtopics.name: Machine identities: client credentials, private_key_jwt, token exchange
subtopics.learn: Service-to-service calls use `grant_type=client_credentials` and the token's `sub` is the service account (Keycloak: `service-account-<client-id>`, after enabling 'Service accounts roles' on the client); prefer `private_key_jwt` client authentication (RFC 7523, `client_assertion_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer`, the client signs a short-lived JWT with its own key) or mTLS (RFC 8705) over a shared `client_secret` that ends up in a `.env` file. When a worker must act for a user after the user's token has expired, do not stash the user's access token in a queue: use RFC 8693 token exchange (`grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange`, `subject_token`, `audience`, `requested_token_type`) at the boundary, or store only (`sub`, `tenant_id`) and run the job under the service identity with the tenant passed explicitly and the authorization decision re-evaluated at execution time. Give each integration its own client so revocation is per-integration, keep secrets in the secret manager (topics 15 and 62), and rotate by creating the new credential before deleting the old one.

subtopics.name: Logout, sessions and back-channel invalidation
subtopics.learn: There are three sessions to end: the IdP's SSO session (Keycloak cookies `KEYCLOAK_IDENTITY` and `KEYCLOAK_SESSION`), your BFF session, and any outstanding tokens. RP-initiated logout redirects to `{end_session_endpoint}?id_token_hint=<id_token>&post_logout_redirect_uri=<uri>&client_id=<id>`, and Keycloak requires that URI to be listed under 'Valid post logout redirect URIs'. Register a 'Backchannel logout URL' on the client: when the IdP ends a session (admin kills it, or the user logs out of another app) Keycloak POSTs a logout token (a JWT whose `events` claim contains `http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout`, plus `sid` and `sub`), which you verify like any JWT and use to delete every BFF session with that `sid`, so store the ID token's `sid` next to the session when you create it. Know that front-channel logout (iframes) breaks under third-party cookie blocking, that deleting your own cookie leaves the SSO session alive so the next visit silently re-logs the user in, and that already-issued access tokens keep working until `exp` unless the API consults a `sid` denylist or introspects.

subtopics.name: Threat model: what RFC 9700 requires and the attack behind each rule
subtopics.learn: Read the OAuth Security BCP as a checklist and map each item to a config line you can point at: exact-string `redirect_uri` matching (no wildcards, no prefix match, no `*` in Keycloak's Valid redirect URIs); PKCE on every code flow; `state` bound to the browser session; `iss` in the authorization response (RFC 9207) to stop mix-up attacks when a client trusts more than one AS; audience-restricted access tokens (`aud`, or the RFC 8707 `resource` parameter) so a token issued for the wiki cannot be replayed at DefenderMate; refresh tokens rotated or sender-constrained (DPoP, RFC 9449, or mTLS); no tokens in URLs; no open redirectors on your own domain that an attacker can chain into a registered `redirect_uri`. Add the JWT-layer items from your verifier: pinned `alg`, `kid` treated as an opaque lookup key (never interpolated into a path or SQL), `jku`/`x5u` ignored, `typ` checked. For each control be able to state the concrete attack it stops in one sentence, because that is exactly the question the customer's AppSec team asks.

resource.label: RFC 9700 - Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security

subtopics.name: Enterprise IdPs in the field: Entra ID, Okta, Google, and brokering
subtopics.learn: You will not choose the IdP; the customer has Entra ID, Okta, Ping or Google Workspace, and sometimes a SAML-only ADFS. Decide between trusting their issuer directly (their `iss`, their JWKS, their claim names in your verifier) and brokering through Keycloak as an identity provider (Keycloak federates to their OIDC or SAML IdP, maps attributes with Identity Provider Mappers, and your API trusts exactly one issuer regardless of customer). Learn the Entra specifics that break integrations: `tid` is their directory id (not your app tenant), `oid` is the stable user id while `sub` is pairwise per app, v1.0 and v2.0 tokens have different `iss` (`https://sts.windows.net/{tid}/` vs `https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tid}/v2.0`) and `aud` formats (`api://<app-id>` vs the client id), app roles arrive in `roles` only after assignment in the enterprise application, and a user in more than 200 groups gets an overage indicator (`_claim_names`/`_claim_sources`) instead of `groups`. Okta gotchas: the org authorization server issues access tokens you cannot validate locally (use a custom authorization server), and `groups` needs a claim filter. Provision users just-in-time on first login keyed on (`iss`, `sub`), never on email, and ask for SCIM or a nightly directory sync for deprovisioning.

resource.label: Microsoft Entra - Access token claims reference

subtopics.name: Debugging auth in a customer environment
subtopics.learn: Start with `curl -s $ISSUER/.well-known/openid-configuration | jq .` to confirm the issuer the IdP believes it is, then decode without verifying (`python3 -c 'import jwt, sys; print(jwt.decode(sys.argv[1], options={"verify_signature": False}))' "$TOKEN"`) and compare `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `typ` and `kid` against what the API expects; never paste a production token into a web decoder. Know the canonical messages and their fixes: `invalid_redirect_uri` (scheme, host, port, trailing slash, `localhost` vs `127.0.0.1` differing from the registered value); `invalid_grant` at the token endpoint (code reused, older than the client login timeout, `redirect_uri` differs from the authorize request, PKCE verifier mismatch, refresh token already rotated); 'Invalid audience' (missing Audience mapper); `iss` mismatch (Keycloak behind a proxy issuing `http://keycloak:8080/...` because `KC_HOSTNAME` and `KC_PROXY_HEADERS` are unset); 'token used before issued' or instant expiry (clock skew on the customer VM: check `chronyc tracking`, then add `leeway`); CORS failure on `/token` from a SPA (Web origins); `unauthorized_client` (grant type disabled on the client). Turn on Keycloak's login and admin event logging (Realm settings -> Events -> Save events) to read the server-side reason instead of guessing from the client's generic error.

resource.label: Keycloak - All configuration options (KC_HOSTNAME, KC_PROXY_HEADERS, KC_DB)

outcomes: You can stand up Keycloak with Docker Compose, create the realm, the confidential BFF client and the audience-restricted API client, export the realm JSON, and have a fresh checkout log in end to end via `--import-realm` in under 15 minutes without opening the admin console.

You can draw the authorization code + PKCE + BFF sequence from memory with every parameter (`response_type`, `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `scope`, `state`, `nonce`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method`, `code`, `code_verifier`) and, for each, name the attack it defeats in one sentence.

You can write the FastAPI verifier dependency (pinned `RS256`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp` with leeway of at most 30 seconds, required claims, RFC 6750 `WWW-Authenticate` errors) and show a test suite in which `alg=none`, HS256 key confusion, wrong `aud`, wrong `iss`, expired, future `nbf`, tampered payload and an ID token presented as an access token are each rejected with the expected `error` value.

You can pass an authorization-matrix test (2 tenants x 3 roles x every route) with zero cross-tenant reads, including URL tenant swaps and `X-Tenant-Id` header spoofing, then delete the application-level `WHERE tenant_id` filter and show Postgres RLS still returns zero foreign rows.

You can explain to a non-engineer security reviewer in under three minutes why the browser holds only an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` session cookie, why PKCE is on for a confidential client, and what is and is not revocable before `exp`, and have them repeat it back correctly.

You can rotate Keycloak's realm signing key under load and show a flat 401 line in Grafana because the verifier refetches JWKS on an unknown `kid`, then state the safe ordering (publish new key, wait the longest token lifetime, remove old key).

You can take an Entra ID or Okta token a customer pastes into a ticket and, within a minute, name why the API rejects it (v1 vs v2 `iss`, `api://` vs client-id `aud`, unassigned app roles, groups overage, opaque org-server token) and the exact setting that fixes it.

You can implement refresh-token rotation and back-channel logout so that replaying a used refresh token revokes the family and an admin-initiated Keycloak logout kills the BFF session on the next request, and demonstrate both with curl.
failureModes: Keycloak behind the customer's ALB mints tokens with `iss` = `http://keycloak:8080/realms/prod` because `KC_HOSTNAME` and `KC_PROXY_HEADERS` were never set; every token fails the API's issuer check after the go-live DNS cutover, and the on-call 'fix' is to remove `issuer=` from `jwt.decode`, which stays in production for a year.

The API validates signature and `exp` but not `aud` because Keycloak's default token says `aud: account` and nobody added the Audience mapper; a token minted for the customer's internal wiki client in the same realm is accepted by DefenderMate's API and a contractor with wiki access lists alert data.

`tenant_id` is read from an `X-Tenant-Id` header 'because the frontend already sends it' and the token claim is never compared; the customer's pentest changes the header and reads another tenant's HubSpot write history, which is a breach notification and a renewal conversation, not a bug.

The IdP rotates its signing key on the first Sunday of the quarter; the API fetched JWKS once at startup with no refetch on unknown `kid`, so every pod returns 401 at 03:00 until someone restarts the deployment, and the incident is misdiagnosed as an IdP outage for 40 minutes.

A Temporal workflow stores the analyst's access token in its input so an activity can call the API 40 minutes later; it is expired, so the realm's Access Token Lifespan is bumped to 24 hours to make the demo work, and every leaked token is now a day-long credential.

The local user table is keyed on email; the customer's Okta admin changes an employee's address during a domain migration, JIT provisioning creates a second account, the old one keeps `tenant_admin`, and the audit trail for a disputed reclassification is split across two identities nobody can reconcile.

Full group paths and every client role are mapped into the access token and the BFF stores the whole token in the session cookie; for the customer's IT director, who is in 60 groups, the cookie exceeds 4096 bytes, the browser drops it, and only that one person is stuck in a login loop, on demo day.
interviewQuestions: A customer's security reviewer asks why your confidential backend uses PKCE when it already authenticates with a client secret. Explain the authorization-code injection attack, what `state` and `nonce` already cover, and what PKCE adds on top.

DefenderMate will be sold to 30 customers, each with their own IdP: Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace and one on-prem ADFS that only speaks SAML. Design login and tenant-claim handling.
